channel.title: ResearchBuzz - Transformed
channel.description: News and resources covering social media, search engines, databases, archives, and other such information collections. Since 1998.

item.title: The Hong Kong Chinese Merchants Collection: An Introduction and its Potential Applications
item.description: The Digital Orientalist: “From the late 19th century onwards, the Hong Kong Chinese merchants were instrumental in shaping the social, political, and business landscapes of Hong Kong, South China, and the overseas Chinese communities around the world. Their commercial practices and business networks have long captivated both public and academic interest. Existing research, however, rarely incorporates firm-level data or merchants’ personal papers.”

item.title: NEARBY HISTORY: UI launches digital collection of reporter Ben J. Plastino
item.description: Moscow-Pullman Daily News: “This spring the University of Idaho Library launched a new digital collection that offers a unique window into the political, social and journalistic history of Idaho in the latter half of the 20th century. Built from the papers of Ben J. Plastino, a longtime reporter and editor for the Idaho Falls Post Register, the digital collection reflects more than five decades of close observation of Idaho’s political landscape.”

item.title: What happened to Omegle? The rise and fall of the internet’s favorite stranger danger
item.description: Mashable: “In 2009, Omegle launched with a simple premise: connect strangers from around the world one-on-one via text or video chat. The pairing was random, and anyone with internet access could join for free, no account required…. But not everyone came to Omegle with good intentions. After it shut down for good in 2023, longtime users were left wondering: what happened to Omegle? We’re here to tell you.”

item.title: STEM creators are working with researchers in all 50 states to showcase ‘Science Across America’
item.description: Tubefilter: “The United States is celebrating its 250th birthday this summer, and a group of creators is turning that milestone into a celebration of science. A nonprofit called the Independent Media Initiative (IMI) is behind 50×50: Science Across America, a coast-to-coast ‘YouTube project’ that will pair influential STEM creators with scientists from all 50 states.”

item.title: From catfishing to patronizing takes on her appearance by a looksmaxxer, this woman just went through the holy grail of tinder date fails
item.description: The Mary Sue: “A woman’s Tinder date with a self-proclaimed “looksmaxxer” turned into a nightmare when the supposed 6’3″ influencer she’d been talking to for six months showed up as a 5’6″ catfish who spent their entire ramen meal critiquing her face.”

item.title: Crypto scam lures ships into Strait of Hormuz, falsely promising safe passage
item.description: Ars Technica: “Crypto scammers are targeting the thousands of ships stranded near the Strait of Hormuz—and at least one ship that faced Iranian gunfire may have been tricked into believing it had paid Iran for safe passage.”

item.title: Kremlin forcing big firms to join ‘witch-hunt’ against internet rebels, claims report
item.description: The Guardian: “Major Russian companies have been conscripted into a ‘witch-hunt’ against users trying to circumvent online controls, researchers have said, as the Kremlin continues trying to cut its citizens off from the global internet.”

item.title: Artificial intelligence flatters users into bad behavior
item.description: PsyPost: “Artificial intelligence systems tend to excessively agree with and validate users, even when those users describe engaging in harmful or unethical behavior. People who interact with these highly agreeable chatbots become more convinced they are right and less willing to apologize during interpersonal conflicts.”

item.title: Ink to link: Ancient script goes online
item.description: Bangalore Mirror: “In a major step to safeguard Karnataka’s rich cultural and intellectual heritage, the state government has initiated the process of establishing a dedicated authority for preserving and digitising ancient manuscripts. The move aims to systematically preserve handwritten records that reflect the state’s history, traditions and knowledge systems, and to make them accessible to future generations.”

item.title: Texas A&M opens world’s largest academic controlled-explosions lab
item.description: Texas A&M University: “It’s seemingly over before it even begins, leaving scientists chasing physics the eye can barely follow. Now, after years of planning, construction and anticipation, scientists at Texas A&M University can finally capture those fleeting, violent moments with a front-row seat inside the world’s largest academic controlled-explosions lab, the newly opened Detonation Research Test Facility (DRTF).” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Largest genomic dataset of Indigenous Americans to date sheds light on history, diversity and health
item.description: Arizona State University: “In a new study published today in Nature, an international team led by the Institute of Evolutionary Biology, with partners at the University of São Paulo and Arizona State University, analyzed genomes from Indigenous populations spanning North America to Patagonia. The result is the largest dataset of its kind, helping researchers trace the genetic threads of ancestry across the Americas.”

item.title: Digitized Copy of 1478 Ptolemy’s ‘Geography’ Available Online
item.description: University of Wisconsin Milwaukee: “Thanks to the work of Digital Collections & Initiatives, the American Geographical Society Library has recently made available a digitized 1478 copy of Ptolemy’s Geography. The AGSL holds over 30 volumes from copies of Ptolemy’s Geography, with this digitization marking the tenth volume digitized, and digital access to the oldest volume in the collection.”

item.title: Claude can now connect to lifestyle apps like Spotify, Instacart and AllTrails
item.description: Engadget: “Anthropic is expanding its directory of connected services for its Claude AI chatbot. The platform can now link up with your accounts on AllTrails, Audible, Booking.com, Instacart, Intuit Credit Karma, Intuit TurboTax, Resy, Spotify, StubHub, Taskrabbit, Thumbtack, TripAdvisor, Uber, Uber Eats and Viator. Additional services will be added in the future.”

item.title: ChatGPT ads expand to logged-out users
item.description: Search Engine Land: “Early reports suggest ads are now appearing seamlessly within conversations for unauthenticated users, even though OpenAI hasn’t formally announced the change. The ads are integrated into chat responses rather than displayed as traditional banners.”

item.title: I replaced Lightroom with this free app and I only miss it a little
item.description: MakeUseOf: “So if you’re tired of spending hundreds of dollars, at the very least, to be able to edit a few photos, you’re using the wrong program. There’s a photo-editing app so good that it can easily replace Lightroom, and you give up only one thing in return.”

item.title: An OpenAI-linked news outlet appears to be entirely AI-generated
item.description: Mashable: “A new report from The Midas Project’s Model Republic publication has found that news site, The Wire by Acutus, relies almost entirely on AI-generated content. The publication has been operational since the end of 2025 with nearly 100 published articles across tech, energy, media, science, business, and healthcare.”

item.title: Peers approve funding for Grenfell Tower archive and preservation works
item.description: International Fire & Safety Journal: “The House of Lords has passed the Grenfell Tower Memorial (Expenditure) Bill to provide statutory authority for the construction and long-term management of a permanent memorial at the tower site.”

item.title: The Indian government says it wants to crack down on fake news. Critics worry it wants to censor content creators–and everyone else.
item.description: Tubefilter: “Basically, the proposal boils down to this: If passed, it would allow the Indian government (specifically its Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology) to have control over social media posts it deemed to be about ‘news and current affairs.’ If a person’s post was judged to be inaccurate or unethical, it would be removed–and the platform they posted on could also face consequences.”

item.title: UK publishers urge CMA to curb Google as search giant claims AI does them no harm
item.description: Press Gazette: “News publishers have disputed a claim from Google that using their content to ‘fine-tune’ its AI models contains ‘no realistic prospect of harm’ to them. ‘Fine-tuning’ enables an AI model that has already been trained to add new data to respond to a specific prompt or task.”

item.title: Short video addiction is linked to lower life satisfaction through loneliness and anxiety
item.description: PsyPost: “A new study published The Journal of Psychology provides evidence that problematic use of short video platforms is linked to higher feelings of loneliness, which subsequently relate to elevated anxiety and a decrease in a person’s contentment with their life.”

item.title: Total solar eclipse led to seismic quiet for cities within its path
item.description: ScienceDaily: “As the Moon swallowed the Sun during the April 8, 2024, total solar eclipse, something remarkable happened on the ground—cities went eerily quiet. Scientists analyzing seismic data found that human-generated vibrations, usually caused by traffic, construction, and daily activity, dropped sharply during totality. The effect was so pronounced that it created a clear ‘seismic hush’ across urban areas directly in the eclipse’s path, before quickly rebounding afterward.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: New app using AI aims to expand civic engagement in Minnesota
item.description: MinnPost: “For anyone who isn’t familiar with how legislation is written and advanced at the state Capitol, the process can feel like it was deliberately created to confuse. Enter CivicLoon, an app that uses artificial intelligence created by a local programmer with the aim of closing that gap between what elected representatives are doing and what their constituents can see and understand.”

item.title: Uncover the Stories of Arkansas WWI Heroes!
item.description: Fold3: “We are excited to announce our new collection of Arkansas WWI Discharge Records (1917-1919), documenting the service of over 70,000 soldiers, sailors, and Marines.”

item.title: This free app makes journaling so easy that I’ve managed to do it for 3 months
item.description: ZDNet: “Diarly has the perfect collection of features, so you don’t feel like it’s missing anything. Neither is the feature list overwhelming. You can install Diarly and immediately start journaling, which is exactly what I did.”

item.title: Why don’t people recycle old smartphones?
item.description: Mashable: “For years, environmental activists have proposed a much easier solution: Simply stop buying so many new electronic devices. Refurbish programs have risen in popularity among tech companies, retail giants, and even the U.S. president, while Right to Repair advocates push for laws that will allow more individuals to extend the life of their personal devices. But even amid these trends, the number of participants needs to multiply tenfold to address the growing e-waste problem.”

item.title: Stale gov.uk pages are feeding AI overviews old data and Brits are believing it
item.description: The Register: “AI overviews from the likes of Google are serving up false summaries of UK government information by drawing on stale GOV.UK pages, according to content designers at the Department for Business and Trade (DBT). The problem, senior content designer Giorgio Di Tunno and content operations lead Neil Starr wrote in a GOV.UK blog post, is that outdated pages no longer maintained are now being actively scraped to answer user queries.”

item.title: Google Uses Cox Ruling to Kill Last Copyright Claim in Textbook Piracy Lawsuit
item.description: TorrentFreak: “Google is trying to put an end to the copyright liability claim in its textbook piracy battle with several academic publishers. In a motion for partial judgment filed in a New York federal court, Google argues that the recent Supreme Court ruling in Cox v. Sony has effectively killed the copyright liability arguments. That is, unless the publishers can prove Google specifically ‘induced’ infringement or built a service ‘tailored’ exclusively for piracy.”

item.title: New York sues Coinbase and Gemini Titan, calls their prediction markets illegal gambling
item.description: Reuters: “New York’s attorney general sued Coinbase Financial Markets and Gemini Titan on Tuesday, claiming their prediction markets violate state laws against illegal gambling.”

item.title: Mississippi’s Air Quality Is Worsening Amid AI Data Center Boom, Report Finds
item.description: Mississippi Free Press: “Air quality has declined in metropolitan areas across Mississippi, with some counties ranking among the nation’s worst for various pollutants, new research from the American Lung Association shows.”

item.title: More realistic content may reduce social media harms for new moms
item.description: University of Nebraska-Lincoln: “Scrolling through picture-perfect portrayals of motherhood may be doing real harm to moms, but a new study from University of Nebraska–Lincoln media scholar Ciera Kirkpatrick shows a ‘dose of reality’ may mitigate some of the damage.”

item.title: Sidewalk troubles? Meet the vigilante artist on a pothole-beautifying spree
item.description: Verite News: “The Pothole Bandit, who posts their joyful, themed and often strange creations on Instagram to their small but mighty following of 17,000, has been doing DIY roadwork for three years in their hometown of Buffalo, New York. Lately, they have been expanding their practice by taking their work on the road, quite literally, as they have travelled to cities including Portland, Oregon, Chattanooga, Tennessee, and Birmingham, Alabama.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: PM Modi says over 20 crore historical records now accessible online through Abhilekh Patal portal
item.description: IANS: “Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Sunday said that the National Archives of India has created a unique digital database through its dedicated Abhilekh Patal Portal, enabling access to over 20 crore invaluable documents related to India’s history.”

item.title: Blenheim Palace digitises centuries-old archive collection
item.description: Oxford Mail: “The Blenheim Archives has finished cataloguing and digitising a collection of material never before seen by the public. The project has brought to light more than 200 documents and revealed fresh detail about life in the villages of Wolvercote, Cutteslowe, and Godstow.”

item.title: There’s a new tool to track how N.J. spends your tax dollars
item.description: WHYY: “The website provides information about state-funded programs and revenue sources, as well as a tool that breaks down state spending and revenue in the current proposed fiscal year 2027 budget. The site also provides information on how much agencies and departments have spent over the past 10 years and an overview of the budget process state lawmakers follow.”

item.title: Illinois Launches Online Resources For Households On Federal Food Assistance
item.description: Block Club Chicago: “Ahead of an estimated 150,000 Illinois households losing access to federal food assistance on May 1, Illinois launched two websites aimed at providing work, training and volunteer hours to those households. Job Ready IL collects training programs and employment opportunities, while Serve Illinois shares volunteer opportunities.”

item.title: Activating the Collection: HathiTrust’s Strategy for Stewardship and Growth
item.description: HathiTrust: “At the 2025 Member Meeting in Brief last fall, and briefly at the 2025 Community Week session ‘Building the HathiTrust Collection Through Special Collections,’ we announced a new HathiTrust Collection Strategy. The completion of this strategy was a long time coming, guided by past work and future thinking.”

item.title: TikTok tests AI Remix option. What it is, how to opt out.
item.description: Mashable: “With remixes on, any public content can be used by its viewers to create digitally generated images, text-based memes, and more. The reveal and lack of notification stirred widespread concern about privacy and consent. Many wondered where the setting came from — and how to turn it off ASAP.”

item.title: Trump’s crypto luncheon draws ‘superstars.’ But his token hovers near low
item.description: Wall Street Journal: This link goes to an MSN-syndicated article and has no paywall. “President Trump feted the biggest holders of his namesake memecoin on Saturday, cheering on a crypto market still fighting through a monthslong slump. In a wide-ranging address from his Mar-a-Lago resort, Trump touched on everything from the Iran war and his crypto friendly policies to the future of artificial intelligence and a recent rally in the shares of Intel, the chip maker in which the U.S. government invested.”

item.title: Heated Rivalry, The Housemaid and Fourth Wing: TikTok launches BookTok bestseller list
item.description: BBC: “From rapid-fire reviews to emotional reactions, creators are shaping reading habits at scale and #BookTok has more than 77 million posts. Now, this influence is being formalised with the launch of the UK’s first official #BookTok bestseller list.”

item.title: Musk v. Altman heads to court next week. Here’s what’s at stake
item.description: CNBC: “Jury selection in Musk v. Altman begins Monday in a federal courthouse in Oakland, just over the Bay Bridge from San Francisco, where OpenAI is headquartered. Should he succeed, Musk said, he wants the court to return all ‘ill-gotten gains’ to OpenAI’s nonprofit, not to him personally. He’s also seeking to have Altman and Brockman removed from their roles and to ‘unwind OpenAI’s for-profit conversion and restructuring.'”

item.title: EU sanctions Russian cultural figures involved with illegal archaeological excavations in occupied Crimea
item.description: Kyiv Independent: “In a move to underscore its commitment to Ukraine’s cultural heritage, the European Union on April 23 included four Russian cultural figures in its 20th sanctions package for their roles in archaeological excavations in occupied Crimea.”

item.title: This vibe-coded tool tells dog owners when pavement is too hot for paws
item.description: Trendwatching: “The tool is simple. Punch in a city or let it detect your location, and Pawmometer pulls real-time weather data to calculate how hot different surfaces are likely to get.”

item.title: Newly-released records detail federal response to Portland ICE protests
item.description: Oregon Public Broadcasting: “Newly released court documents detail federal officers’ first-hand accounts of protest activity and what led them to use force outside the Immigration and Customs Enforcement building in Portland over the summer and fall.”

item.title: Microsoft’s GitHub grounds Copilot account sign-ups amid capacity crunch
item.description: The Register: “Microsoft’s GitHub has stopped accepting new Copilot individual subscriptions while the code hosting biz figures out how it can meet its service commitments without breaking the bank.”

item.title: Outrage in China after streaming site debuts AI actor ‘database’
item.description: Straits Times: “China’s equivalent of Netflix, iQIYI, faced backlash on April 20 over a new initiative that facilitates the use of actors’ likenesses in artificially generated dramas and films. More than 100 celebrities have joined a platform to connect with makers of AI-generated content interested in using their image, a senior executive told a conference in Beijing.”

item.title: Federal judge blocks reworked Arkansas law restricting minors’ social media
item.description: Arkansas Advocate: “A federal judge has temporarily blocked an Arkansas law set to take effect Tuesday that would have restricted minors’ social media access. Tech industry trade group NetChoice in January filed a lawsuit challenging Act 900 of 2025, which sought to amend a 2023 law found to be unconstitutional.”

item.title: Maryland property search tool goes offline after cyber threat
item.description: Maryland Matters: “Maryland’s online property records database has been offline for nearly a week following a cybersecurity breach, according to a statement from the State Department of Assessments and Taxation. State officials believe that compromised systems only included public records that users could already find on the SDAT property search webpage, according to the news release, issued Saturday.”

item.title: Tokyo court rules movie and anime ‘spoiler articles’ are copyright infringement in landmark criminal case — detailed, monetized plot summaries land man in Japanese prison
item.description: Tom’s Hardware: “In a new landmark ruling, the Tokyo District Court has sentenced 39-year-old Wataru Takeuchi to 1.5 years in prison and imposed a 1 million Yen ($6,300) fine for posting ‘spoiler articles.’ The defendant ran a website that shared detailed plot summaries of movies and anime, often describing the entire story from start to finish. Prosecutors argued these articles were infringing on copyright because of their strenuous detail.”

item.title: What we measured, and how, in our indicators map
item.description: Greater Greener Washington: “Funding from the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation’s Local Data for Equitable Communities program, and technical support from the Urban Institute, has enabled us to produce an interactive choropleth map aggregating 23 indicators — including demographics, housing production, building permits, traffic safety, infrastructure access, and air quality — across a variety of geographies.”

item.title: Antigravity Is Preserving Historical Sites in 3D Using its 360° Drone
item.description: PetaPixel: “Antigravity has announced Project Eternal, a global initiative unveiled following the International Day for Monuments and Sites, aimed at preserving cultural heritage through advanced imaging and Gaussian Splatting. The project brings together drone technology, panoramic capture systems, and 3D reconstruction tools to create accessible digital archives of historically significant locations.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Checkmate! Dominate the Competition by Learning Game Theory with Wolfram Language
item.description: Wolfram Blog: “I am glad to announce the launch of Introduction to Game Theory, a free interactive course that aims to teach computational game theory to anyone. This course gives the computational basis for the many daily, social and human applications of this branch of mathematics.”

item.title: SFP and Hilborn Lab launch 8th edition of the Fishery Improvement Projects Database
item.description: Sustainable Fisheries Partnership: “Sustainable Fisheries Partnership (SFP) and the Hilborn Lab at the University of Washington have released the 8th version of the Fishery Improvement Projects Database (FIP-DB), marking another major step forward in providing structured data to help track the evolution, scale, and performance of fishery improvement projects (FIPs) worldwide.”

item.title: OpenAI Unveils New Image Generator to Usher in an AI Slop ‘Renaissance’
item.description: Gizmodo: “OpenAI just unveiled a brand new image generator that it claims can churn out smarter and more precise slop than ever before. ChatGPT Images 2.0 is going to be a ‘renaissance’ in AI image generation, according to an introductory promo ad that ran before OpenAI’s livestream on Tuesday announcing the news.”

item.title: Elon Musk’s near-daily online posts about race are turning off some fans
item.description: Washington Post: This link goes to a Yahoo-syndicated version of the article with no paywall. “Over the past seven months, 6 percent of Musk’s posts on X, a total of about 850, have been about race, nearly triple the rate for the previous two years. More than half of those posts have used the word ‘white.’ The billionaire has posted on X about race nearly daily – 166 out of 197 days – from last October to mid-April, The Post analysis found.”

item.title: Visa’s U.K. “creator card” aims to combat cashflow issues while upping TikTok Live payouts
item.description: Tubefilter: “Creators based in the U.K. can now take advantage of a banking solution that serves their unique financial needs. Visa has partnered with TikTok to launch a debit card that offers a number of creator-centric perks.”

item.title: US freezes $344 million in cryptocurrency said to be linked to Iran
item.description: CNN: “The Trump administration has frozen $344 million in cryptocurrency it says was linked to Iran as the United States ratchets up pressure on Tehran. The move, first reported by CNN, comes as shaky diplomatic efforts to reach a deal to end the war continue to stall and the global economy reels from its impact.”

item.title: Trump administration vows crackdown on Chinese companies ‘exploiting’ AI models made in U.S.
item.description: Associated Press: “The Trump administration is vowing to crack down on foreign tech companies’ exploitation of U.S. artificial intelligence models, singling out China at a time that country is narrowing the gap with the U.S. in the AI race.”

item.title: Missouri House forges ahead with bill targeting AI deepfakes and youth social media use
item.description: Missouri Independent: “The legislation would require social media companies to implement age verification measures and prohibit them from targeting youth with ‘manipulative or addictive’ design features. It would also make it a felony to share deepfakes.”

item.title: USDA Moves to Shutter Maryland Research Facility
item.description: NOTUS: “The Agriculture Department announced plans Thursday to shut down a massive federal research complex in Prince George’s County, Maryland, over the objection of members of Congress. The department will begin decommissioning the Beltsville Agricultural Research Center, a 6,500-acre federal research complex that has operated since 1910 and is considered the world’s largest agricultural research facility.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: 250 Million Trees!
item.description: Ecosia Blog: “We’ve built the world’s largest network of local reforestation organizations, 125 organizations and over 200,000 tree planters — supporting livelihoods, local knowledge, and long-term forest stewardship.”

item.title: How to Spot AI Audiobooks on Libby
item.description: Lifehacker: “Library digital lending app Libby says it does not make decisions when it comes to AI-generated content on its platform; rather, the app simply serves to make available to borrowers the content that libraries themselves have purchased. That means if you’re passionate about your stand against AI-generated books and audiobooks, you may want to give your feedback to your local library. And if you want to avoid listening to AI-generated audiobooks from Libby, there’s a simple way to spot them.”

item.title: AI streaming is going mainstream in China, whether audiences want it or not
item.description: DigitalTrends: “At its annual content showcase in Beijing, founder and CEO Gong Yu announced that iQiyi is pivoting its popular streaming platform into a social media destination built around AI-generated content. Alongside the announcement, the company debuted Nadou Pro, an AI tool, which, according to the company, is capable of handling almost every aspect of filmmaking, from scriptwriting and storyboards to the final video delivery.”

item.title: Man with @ihackedthegovernment Instagram account tells judge, “I made a mistake”
item.description: Ars Technica: “A 25-year-old Tennessee man avoided prison time after pleading guilty to accessing government systems with stolen login credentials and boasting of the deed on an Instagram account with the handle, @ihackedthegovernment.”

item.title: A $5 Bluetooth tracker hidden in a postcard exposed a warship’s movements
item.description: TechSpot: “Journalist Just Vervaart concealed a Bluetooth tracker inside a postcard. He then mailed it to the vessel using publicly available instructions from the Dutch Ministry of Defense, intended to help families send mail to loved ones stationed on the ship. This protocol provided enough details to get the tracker aboard the ship.”

item.title: Mastodon says its flagship server was hit by a DDoS attack
item.description: TechCrunch: “Mastodon’s flagship server was hit by a distributed denial-of-service attack on Monday, the social networking software maker said, which rendered the instance unusable at times. Much of the site was inaccessible, throwing error messages or displaying a full-screen outage warning.”

item.title: Licensing Best Practices for the Sharing of Scientific Data
item.description: Creative Commons: “Today, we are sharing our newest report, Licensing Best Practices for Sharing Scientific Data. This report builds on our 2023 report Recommended Best Practices for the Better Sharing of Climate Data with the goal of extending the open data practices originally designed for climate data to other disciplines.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Vietnam launches upgraded National Database on Legal Documents
item.description: VietnamNet: “In the coming time, the database is envisioned as a leading digital legal knowledge platform based on five strategic pillars, including full digitalisation of the legal document lifecycle, an interconnected legal data ecosystem, expanded AI use for legal analysis and alerts, a national big data platform on law, and broader digital legal knowledge for society at large.”

item.title: This Creative Studio Released a “Ciggiedex” of Chinese Cigarette Brands
item.description: RADII: “…spend a few minutes on the site and it clicks: this isn’t really about cigarettes. It’s about documentation, aesthetics, and the growing instinct among young Chinese creators to catalog the overlooked.”

item.title: Launching XOXO Explore
item.description: XOXO: “Named after what we thought would be a throwaway title for a short-lived GitHub repo, allow us to introduce XOXO Explore. Each festival year now has its own index, featuring the complete lineup of every speaker, performer, artist, and project from that year, along with a detailed (and accurate!) schedule with descriptions, dates, times, and venues meticulously imported from our print attendee guide.”

item.title: China’s DeepSeek releases preview of long-awaited V4 model as AI race intensifies
item.description: CNBC: “Chinese artificial intelligence startup DeepSeek on Friday released a preview version of its long-awaited V4 large language model, allowing users to test its new capabilities and features.”

item.title: Trump picked a fight with Anthropic. Now the administration is backing off.
item.description: Politico: “Just two months after President Donald Trump declared a government-wide blacklist of the tech startup’s AI software, cybersecurity worries tied to the company’s powerful new Mythos model have both sides searching for a ceasefire, according to six tech lobbyists and policy experts, including two with ties to the White House.”

item.title: deviantART says artists made $23 million on its platform last year, boasts that it was “100% right” to embrace generative AI
item.description: Tubefilter: “Will we see deviantART be a creator economy force alongside YouTube and TikTok in 2026? Thousands of artists are looking for a new home platform after X’s descent into Grokland–but will they be willing to make money on a website that is still doggedly pro-AI?”

item.title: The Iranian women Trump ‘saved’ from execution are simultaneously real and AI-manipulated
item.description: The Verge: “The collage that Trump posted is, at the very least, AI-modified, Mahsa Alimardani, the associate director of the Technology Threats & Opportunities program at WITNESS, told The Verge. But the women themselves are real.”

item.title: Kevin Weil and Bill Peebles exit OpenAI as company continues to shed ‘side quests’
item.description: TechCrunch: “OpenAI is losing two of the architects of its most ambitious moonshots. Kevin Weil, who led the company’s science research initiative, and Bill Peebles, the researcher behind AI video tool Sora, both announced their departures on Friday.”

item.title: US soldier charged with using classified intel to win $400K Polymarket bet on Maduro raid
item.description: Associated Press: “A U.S. special forces soldier involved in the military operation to capture Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro has been charged with using classified information about the mission to win more than $400,000 in an online betting market, federal officials announced Thursday.”

item.title: Brazil regulator approves deeper probe into Google’s news content use
item.description: Reuters: “Brazil’s antitrust watchdog CADE approved on Thursday a recommendation to deepen ​investigations into the use of journalistic content ‌by Alphabet’s Google, which would assess potential abuse of the company’s dominant market position.”

item.title: Ombudsman column: The Pentagon is trying to silence me
item.description: Stars and Stripes: “No one should be surprised that they’re kicking out the one person charged by Congress with protecting Stars and Stripes’ editorial independence. For nearly a year, Pentagon leadership has placed more and more restrictions on the mainstream media. The New York Times sued and when the Defense/War Department lost in court, instead of following the judge’s ruling Secretary Hegseth and company pivoted, finding another way to restrict journalists. The judge rejected that attempt, too.”

item.title: UK government records relating to Troubles published by National Archives
item.description: Irish Legal News: “This first batch of files includes records offering fresh insights into the conflict’s early stages, including: the Civil Rights Campaign; the Outbreak of Conflict and the deployment of the Army; and the establishment of the Northern Ireland Office (NIO) in 1972 following the suspension of Stormont.”

item.title: New Coaching Database and License System
item.description: Athletics Ireland: “Athletics Ireland is pleased to announce the launch of its new Coaching Database and License System, designed to enhance the support, recognition, and governance of coaching across the organisation. … Under the new system, all coaches who are registered members of Athletics Ireland, hold a Level 2 or Level 3 coaching qualification, and have completed Garda Vetting will be officially recognised as Licensed Coaches.”

item.title: Bluesky set out to fix social media. Now it’s running into familiar problems
item.description: Fast Company: “Once lauded as the heroic anti-X, a more principled and moralistic Twitterverse, Bluesky now appears to be struggling to retain users and build a sustainable, competitive business model. Its identity as an alternative to Twitter drew in waves of oppositional voices, often labeled ‘Resistance Twitter,’ but that positioning may now be its biggest hurdle.”

item.title: BU students react to OpenAI’s Sora shutdown with relief, fear about artist livelihoods
item.description: The Daily Free Press (Boston University): “Although OpenAI did not provide a concrete reason for terminating Sora, it appears the shutdown was largely driven by financial factors, according to The New York Times. OpenAI earned about $13 billion in revenue, but it expects to spend about $100 billion over the next four years. Theo Hanson, a freshman health science major at Boston University with a minor in fine arts, said the shutdown came as a genuine surprise — but a welcome one.”

item.title: Berlin Museum Oversees Digital Resurrection of Hundreds of Paintings Destroyed During World War II
item.description: ARTNews: “Hundreds of paintings lost to the ravages of war—including multiple works by Peter Paul Rubens, Paolo Veronese, Anthony van Dyck, and Caravaggio—will soon be viewable online courtesy of a digitization initiative by Berlin’s Gemäldegalerie.”

item.title: How did thousands of sensitive LAPD files get leaked? City officials seek explanation
item.description: Los Angeles Times: “In the aftermath of a recent data breach that saw hackers make off with a vast trove of confidential police records, Los Angeles leaders have sought an explanation from the city’s top lawyer, whose office was targeted.”

item.title: New undersea cable cutter risks Internet’s backbone
item.description: Ars Technica: “A Chinese ship has tested a new device capable of slicing through submarine data cables thousands of meters beneath the ocean surface. That demonstration may exacerbate security concerns over a spate of suspected sabotage incidents targeting undersea communications and power cables from the Baltic Sea to the Pacific Ocean.”

item.title: Gen Z Workers Pick Human-Only Output Over AI-Assisted
item.description: Search Engine Journal: “Gen Z workers surveyed said they would trust human-only work over AI-assisted output by more than 2-to-1. The findings come from a new survey by the Walton Family Foundation, GSV Ventures and Gallup.”

item.title: Researchers: Chatbots are biased and should not be used for political advice
item.description: University of Copenhagen: “AI Popular chatbots such as ChatGPT and Gemini are not neutral and tend to favor certain political parties when asked who users should vote for. This makes them unsuitable for providing advice in connection with elections, according to researchers from the University of Copenhagen behind a new analysis of political bias in chatbots.”

item.title: How 2 men claimed an absurd record by driving an old 3-wheel car the length of Africa
item.description: Associated Press: “Englishman Ollie Jenks remembers when his friend first pitched the idea to him. ‘It was so ridiculous I couldn’t say no,’ Jenks said. The proposal by his Canadian buddy Seth Scott, a fellow lover of cars and crazy adventures, was for them to drive a decades-old British-made Reliant Robin car from London to the southern tip of Africa — a 14,000-mile (22,500-kilometer) journey through 22 countries — to set a record for the longest trip in a three-wheeled vehicle.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: MIT researchers build the world’s largest collection of Olympiad-level math problems — and open it to everyone
item.description: MIT CSAIL: “MathNet is the largest high-quality dataset of proof-based math problems ever created, and it is not close. Comprising more than 30,000 expert-authored problems and solutions spanning 47 countries, 17 languages, and 143 competitions, it is five times larger than the next biggest dataset of its kind.”

item.title: New online events calendar helps travelers discover what’s happening throughout state
item.description: Big Island Now: “The new feature allows users to browse curated events by island, making it easier to incorporate festivals, cultural experiences and local activities into itineraries. It helps travelers go beyond traditional planning and discover what’s happening during their stay.”

item.title: Ohio Launches Statewide Dashboard to Tackle Chronic Absenteeism
item.description: Governing: “Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine and Department of Education and Workforce Director Stephen Dackin have announced the launch of a statewide Attendance Dashboard in an effort to combat chronic absenteeism in K-12 public schools. Over 25% of Ohio students were chronically absent last year, missing nearly one month of school.” Over 1/4? Holy crap.

item.title: Firefox 150 Is Now Available for Download, This Is What’s New
item.description: 9to5 Linux: “Highlights of Firefox 150 include support for the GTK emoji picker on Linux to let you insert emoji by using the Ctrl+. keyboard shortcut, and the ability to reorganize PDF pages directly in the Firefox PDF viewer, including moving, copying, and deleting pages.”

item.title: Here’s an open-source Google Circle To Search alternative that works offline
item.description: How-To Geek: “Aditya, the developer, has said that his Circle To Search does not require the internet for text recognition, and it can also detect QR codes, and does Smart Scan offline, without requiring uploading these images to Google servers, which is the case with Google’s version.”

item.title: Even Without Internet Access, Prisoners Are Trying to Benefit From A.I.
item.description: New York Times: This link goes to a gift article. “…as hype about the technology has infiltrated prison yards and cellblocks, many inmates are eager to try it out. They’re attending workshops and classes to learn about A.I. They ask friends to send printouts of chatbot answers by snail mail. Some inmates even use contraband cellphones to gain access to the technology. The result? A.I.-generated legal documents, essays, business plans and even a bespoke board game or two.”

item.title: A Woman Is Suing MrBeast’s Company For Alleged Sexual Harassment And Verbal Abuse
item.description: Kotaku: “A woman who previously worked at Beast Industries, the company behind MrBeast’s popular YouTube channel, has filed a lawsuit against the YouTuber’s company claiming she was sexually harassed, verbally abused, and fired after returning from maternity leave. The company says it has extensive evidence that ‘unequivocally refutes her claims.'”

item.title: The White House Intervened on Behalf of Accused Sex Trafficker Andrew Tate During a Federal Investigation
item.description: ProPublica: “Federal authorities were chided for seizing electronic devices from Tate and his brother, and told to return them, records and interviews show. Experts said the intervention was highly inappropriate.”

item.title: Taylor Swift and Bad Bunny top Spotify’s first all-time most streamed artists list
item.description: Associated Press: “It’s her, hi! Taylor Swift has topped Spotify’s first ever list of the most streamed artists of all time, published Thursday morning. She’s followed by Puerto Rican superstar Bad Bunny. That comes as no surprise: In 2025 the artist born Benito Antonio Martínez Ocasio was named the streaming giant’s most played artist of the year for a fourth time, dethroning Swift.”

item.title: Got Bugs? U of G Collecting Samples to Catalogue Canada’s Biodiversity
item.description: University of Guelph: “Whether they’re crawling in the dirt or buzzing around a park, researchers at the University of Guelph want your bugs. It’s part of BugQuest, a nationwide community science project run by the Centre for Biodiversity Genomics (CBG). The goal? To set up 1,000 traps across Canada to survey insect diversity.” Good morning, Internet…
